keySentence: Each sister chose her own path — proving that a woman's worth lies in her character, not convention.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: Society in Louisa May Alcott's time had very specific ideas about what women should do and be. Women were expected to marry well and run a home and not ask for more than that from their lives. The March sisters did not all follow these expectations and the book says that this was completely fine. Meg married for love rather than money and built a happy home without wealth or social standing. Jo refused to marry at all until she found the right person and wrote stories that she truly believed in. Beth lived quietly and fully and Amy pursued her art seriously even when others doubted her talent. Each sister chose her own path — proving that a woman's worth lies in her character, not convention.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: When Little Women was published in 1868 it entered a world with very firm ideas about acceptable female behavior. A woman's worth was measured primarily by her marriage prospects and her ability to create a proper domestic environment. Alcott's novel pushes back against this measurement system not through explicit argument but through sympathetic portraiture. She creates four women who are each worth knowing and each admirable without any of them fully conforming to convention. Meg conforms most closely and is treated with as much warmth as Jo who conforms least — both choices are presented as valid. The novel's implicit argument is that character — honesty, courage, kindness, persistence — is the real measure of a person. Convention tells us which paths are acceptable; character tells us which paths are truly ours to walk without apology. Each sister chose her own path — proving that a woman's worth lies in her character, not convention.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Little Women's feminist argument is embedded so naturally in its narrative that readers often absorb it without noticing. Alcott is not delivering a political treatise — she is telling four stories in which female agency is simply taken for granted. Each March sister is presented as the author of her own life in a way that was genuinely unusual for the fiction of the period. Their choices are not constrained by what society allows but by what they themselves most deeply want and value. When Jo rejects Laurie, she does so on the grounds of her own feelings and her own sense of what her life should be. When Meg accepts John, she does so on the same grounds — not because convention points that way but because her heart does. The parallel structure of these decisions is Alcott's most elegant argument: the freedom to choose is what matters, not the choice. A woman whose domesticity is freely chosen is as liberated as one whose writing career is freely chosen — what matters is the freedom. Each sister chose her own path — proving that a woman's worth lies in her character, not convention.
